passage:
Tuesday. Kashish saw the review of a singer’s new album pop up in a group chat with Himani. Within an hour the fans had turned on the reviewer, calling her ugly and stupid. Himani, usually gentle, added a cruel joke.
Wednesday. Someone posted a link to the reviewer’s workplace and made remarks about her family. Kashish felt sick. Kashish muted the chat, reported the posts, and did not reply.
Friday. Kashish and Himani had lunch together. “I saw you leave that chat,” said Himani quietly. “It felt like a game until the family part. I’m not sure why I joined in.”

qa.q: What did someone post on Wednesday?
qa.a: Someone posted a link to the reviewer's workplace and made remarks about her family.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when the family remarks appeared?
qa.a: Kashish felt sick and upset at the cruelty. Muting, reporting and staying silent show Kashish did not want any part of it.

qa.q: What safe steps did Kashish take instead of joining or arguing in the chat?
qa.a: Kashish muted the chat and reported the posts without replying. Kashish later listened to Himani calmly instead of scolding.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt about the whole thing by Friday?
qa.a: Himani seemed uneasy and a little ashamed, saying it felt like a game until the family part. Himani was asking why the group made it easy to join.

grounding: Shows an adult seeing fans turn abusive online, recognising how group identity allows cruelty, and choosing not to join.

passage:
Dolma, this happened when I was your age. I’m Lokesh, and I belonged to a fan club for a famous batsman. A magazine writer said our hero was past his best, and our club president got furious.
At the Sunday meeting he said we should all write to the writer, as rude as we could. Everyone laughed and agreed. I sat silent, though my ears burned.
Afterwards I told our teacher-patron what was planned. The teacher called the president in. The letters were never sent.
Some boys avoided me for weeks. The writer never knew. I still think about how easy it was for everyone else to say yes.

qa.q: What did the club president want the members to do?
qa.a: The president wanted everyone to write to the writer, as rude as they could.

qa.q: How might the club president have felt when the magazine writer criticised the hero?
qa.a: The president was probably furious and felt personally attacked, since the club was built around the hero. Group loyalty made anger feel like duty.

qa.q: Which choice of Lokesh's stopped the letters, and what did it cost?
qa.a: Lokesh told the teacher-patron about the plan. The letters were never sent, but some boys avoided Lokesh for weeks.

qa.q: What might the magazine writer have gone through if the letters had arrived?
qa.a: The writer would have received a pile of rude letters for one opinion and would probably have felt targeted and unsafe.

grounding: An elder recalls a fan club planning to abuse a critic and choosing not to join, and quietly raising it with a trusted adult.

passage: Usha was on a night shift at the call centre, checking her phone between calls, when the fan page she co-ran for the cricketer Vikram Joshi exploded. A sports writer, Aparna Rao, had called Joshi's captaincy 'selfish'. Fans were posting her home city, photos of her children from an old post, and worse. The other admins wanted to share it all: 'She asked for it.' Usha's stomach dropped. She loved Joshi's batting, but this wasn't cricket. With a queue of customers waiting, she typed fast: 'Deleting anything with her family or address. Criticise the article, not the person.' Two admins called her a traitor. She muted them, reported the worst posts to the platform, and took the next call, hands still shaking.

qa.q: What did Aparna Rao call Joshi's captaincy?
qa.a: 'Selfish'.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she saw the posts about Aparna's family?
qa.a: Her stomach dropped; she felt alarmed and disgusted, knowing it had crossed from criticism into cruelty.

qa.q: What steps did Usha take to refuse to join the harassment?
qa.a: Deleting posts with family or address, telling fans to criticise the article not the person, and reporting the worst posts.

qa.q: What might Aparna Rao be going through that night?
qa.a: Fear and exposure, with strangers sharing her home city and her children's photos because of an opinion.

grounding: An adult fan sees her group abuse a critic's family, recognises how group identity permits cruelty, and refuses to join.

passage: In a Noida café, Yash watched his old friend Jatin scroll and laugh. 'Look what we did to Kavita Rao's brother,' Jatin said. Jatin's fan club, devoted to a rival actor, had flooded the brother's personal account with insults after Kavita, an actress, said something mild about their star. The brother was a college student who had nothing to do with films. 'Join in, it's hilarious.' Yash looked at the comments. Some were jokes. Many were threats. He felt the pull: Jatin was his oldest friend, and the group was huge. 'I'm not doing that,' Yash said quietly. 'He's just some kid.' Jatin rolled his eyes. That night Yash reported the worst comments and messaged the brother: 'Sorry this is happening.'

qa.q: What had Kavita Rao done to anger the fan club?
qa.a: Said something mild about their star.

qa.q: What did Yash feel when Jatin asked him to join in?
qa.a: He felt the pull of loyalty to his oldest friend and the huge group, alongside discomfort at the threats.

qa.q: How did Yash refuse without a big fight?
qa.a: He said quietly that he wouldn't, because the brother was just a kid, then reported the worst comments and sent a kind message.

qa.q: What is it like for Kavita Rao's brother?
qa.a: A college student with nothing to do with films is flooded with insults and threats, likely scared and confused.

grounding: A young man watches a friend's fan club abuse a rival's family, sees how the group permits cruelty, and chooses not to join.

passage:
'Why are you smiling like that?' Sarika asked.
Uday turned his phone round. 'The referee from Sunday's match. Our fan group found his daughter's account.'
Sarika put down her tea. 'His daughter?'
'She posted a birthday photo. People are commenting "your dad's a cheat" under it.' He laughed, then stopped when he saw her face.
'How old is she?'
'I don't know. Fifteen?'
'Uday. You were furious about that penalty, fine. But that's a child.'
He looked at the screen again. 'I didn't write anything.'
'You laughed.'
There was a long silence. 'The group's like that,' Uday said. 'Once one person starts, everyone joins.'
'You don't have to.' Sarika held out her hand. 'Report the comments. Leave the group chat for a while.'
He hesitated, then pressed Report.

qa.q: What were people commenting under the referee's daughter's photo?
qa.a: 'Your dad's a cheat.'

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when she put down her tea?
qa.a: Shocked and upset that the fan group had targeted the referee's daughter, a child.

qa.q: What did Sarika suggest Uday do, and why?
qa.a: Report the comments and leave the group chat for a while, so he stops being part of the pile-on.

qa.q: What does Uday's 'Once one person starts, everyone joins' reveal about how he sees the group?
qa.a: He sees how the group pulls people into cruelty, and admits that laughing along felt normal until Sarika questioned it.

grounding: A woman sees her partner's fan group abuse a referee's child, names the cruelty and refuses to let it pass.

passage: I'm Swati. Last month a film critic, Varun Kulkarni, gave our favourite actor's new film two stars. I'm a fan too, so I was annoyed, and I opened the comments ready to add mine. What I found scared me. Thousands of replies. People posting the area where he lives. Someone had found his wife's profile and was tagging her with insults. Our own fan club group, the one where I share wallpapers, was organising it: "Everyone hit the review at 8 p.m." A friend from the club messaged me, "You in?" It would have been easy. One reply, one more voice in the crowd; nobody would know it was me. I thought of his wife reading it at breakfast. I typed, "No, this isn't what being a fan means," left the group, and reported the posts sharing where he lives.

qa.q: How many stars did Varun Kulkarni give the film?
qa.a: He gave it two stars.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when the friend asked "You in?"
qa.a: Swati was tempted, since joining felt easy and anonymous, but also uneasy and scared by the cruelty.

qa.q: Which steps did Swati take, and why did they help?
qa.a: Swati refused, left the group and reported the posts sharing where he lives, which took one voice out of the crowd and helped protect the critic's family.

qa.q: What is it like for Varun's wife to be tagged by strangers?
qa.a: It is likely frightening and hurtful to be targeted over a film review she didn't even write.

grounding: Swati sees fans abusing a critic and his family online, recognises how group identity permits cruelty, and chooses not to join.
